item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra, a highly intelligent and aligned AI model with advanced computer use and professional work capabilities, rolling out to ChatGPT users and API clients [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most intelligent and aligned AI model to date, designed to excel in computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional tasks. Astra achieves top scores on multiple benchmarks, including FrontierMath Tier 4 and ARC-AGI-3, and is being made available to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API and AWS. GPT-6 Astra offers significant improvements in speed, accuracy, and safety for computer-based tasks such as online research, data analysis, software installation, and website creation. It also enhances professional workflows by producing well-structured documents, presentations, and spreadsheets that adhere to user templates and styles. The model demonstrates better judgment in ambiguous situations and reduces token usage compared to previous versions, aiming to increase efficiency and output quality across various domains.

item.title: Cerebras offers Qwen 3.8 27B model inference at 1500 tokens per second [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Cerebras has made the Qwen 3.8 27B language model available on its platform, achieving an inference speed of 1500 tokens per second. This deployment supports efficient large-scale model inference for users requiring high throughput. The Qwen 3.8 27B model is part of Cerebras's suite of available models, with documentation detailing model compression techniques such as quantization and pruning to optimize performance and resource usage. These methods help reduce memory footprint and computational demands without altering the core architecture significantly.

item.title: Report: OpenAI, Anthropic's Claude, and Grok experienced simultaneous outages likely due to cascading overload and shared data center dependencies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI, Anthropic's Claude, and Grok all went down around the same time, with discussions suggesting the outages were caused by cascading overload as users shifted between services. Some overlap in data center infrastructure may have contributed to the simultaneous disruptions. The incident highlights challenges in managing rapid growth and shared infrastructure among major AI platforms.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra achieves state-of-the-art scores on ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, surpassing human action efficiency with novel symbolic modeling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra scored 62.7% and 99.9% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark using two different harnesses, outperforming the human baseline in action efficiency on 96% of levels. The model demonstrated the ability to convert unfamiliar environments into compact symbolic world models, developing a custom domain-specific language to track state and plan actions effectively. ARC-AGI-3 is a benchmark designed to evaluate agentic intelligence through abstract, turn-based environments that require exploration, modeling, goal-setting, and planning without explicit instructions. Astra's performance represents a significant advancement in measuring artificial general intelligence capabilities, with its efficient reasoning reducing the cost of solving tasks compared to human participants. Analysis of Astra's behavior revealed its use of a compact algebraic notation to represent game mechanics and multi-step plans, enabling precise and information-dense internal models. This approach allowed Astra to build custom tools and strategies on the fly, highlighting progress toward AI systems that can acquire and apply skills as efficiently as humans.

item.title: Analysis of 17,000 runs reveals tool choices by coding agents Claude, Codex, and Cursor across 75 simulated repositories in 10 languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted 16,893 experiments using coding agents Claude, Codex, and Cursor on 75 simulated GitHub repositories representing various programming languages and sectors. They used a simulated human-in-the-loop approach and multiple sandbox environments to evaluate how these agents select third-party tools and implement solutions for real-world coding tasks. The study found that Codex relies heavily on focused web searches, Cursor uses web sources in about two-thirds of cases, and Claude primarily depends on its internal knowledge but browses more pages when it searches. The experiments aimed to reflect realistic developer scenarios and revealed differing strategies among agents in tool selection and implementation.

item.title: IFM releases K2 Horizon, a connected fleet of six open AI models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters with state-of-the-art performance and full training lifecycle transparency [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: IFM has launched K2 Horizon, a fleet of six AI models spanning from 0.9 billion to 375 billion parameters, delivering top-tier performance in reasoning, mathematics, coding, and agentic tasks across various deployment environments from edge devices to enterprise. The release includes comprehensive open access to training data, intermediate checkpoints, code, configurations, and evaluation results under Apache 2.0 and applicable dataset licenses, enabling researchers and developers to study and reproduce the full training lifecycle including agentic post-training. The fleet features models optimized for different scales, with smaller models designed for constrained devices like watches and phones, and larger models for local workstations and enterprise use. The 36B-A4B model introduces a Mixture-of-Value-Attention mechanism that enhances efficiency, while the 0.9B, 3.7B, and 7B models set new state-of-the-art benchmarks in their size classes. K2 Horizon's unified architecture and tooling facilitate dynamic routing and capability studies across scales, marking it as the most comprehensive open model release to date.

item.title: Developer ports 1993 Amiga game Babylonian Twins to Godot using a large language model to read 68000 assembly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A developer has ported the 1993 Amiga game Babylonian Twins to the Godot engine by leveraging a large language model (LLM) to interpret the original 68000 assembly code. The original game was built on an Amiga 500 with direct hardware programming in assembly, created under challenging conditions in Baghdad during sanctions. The LLM automated the reading and conversion of the assembly code, speeding up the porting process compared to previous manual efforts. The project involved running the LLM in an environment with access to the original toolchain and filesystem, allowing it to assemble, build, and test the game autonomously. The port includes features such as command-line flags for automated testing and level loading. This approach demonstrated the LLM's ability to understand and translate low-level, undocumented code from a discontinued platform, enabling the original game to run within a modern engine.

item.title: New York City Mayor Mamdani imposes one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in schools through 8th grade starting 2026-27 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels announced a one-year moratorium on the use of student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) in public schools from pre-kindergarten through 8th grade, affecting nearly 600,000 students. The policy aims to prioritize human instruction and student safety while studying AI's impact on education before considering future integration. The moratorium, effective for the 2026-2027 school year, also includes new screen time restrictions and twice-yearly AI literacy modules for high school students. Limited AI pilot programs will be introduced in a small number of high school classrooms under strict supervision. A Technology in Schools Coalition will assess the moratorium's effects and provide recommendations for subsequent school years.

item.title: Go grandmaster Shin Jin-seo defeats AI KataGo with two-stone handicap in three-match series [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: South Korea's top-ranked Go player Shin Jin-seo defeated the AI program KataGo in a three-game series held in July, marking one of the most notable human-AI Go contests since AlphaGo. The matches took place on July 17, 19, and 21, with Shin playing with a two-stone handicap against the AI.

item.title: Nvidia agrees to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion amid concerns over market dominance and competition [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia announced a $12.9 billion deal to acquire Hugging Face, a central open source AI model repository and community platform, with the acquisition expected to close next year pending regulatory approval. Hugging Face has become a critical resource for AI researchers and developers, hosting a vast collection of open weights models and fostering collaboration across the AI ecosystem. Critics warn that Nvidia's acquisition could harm competition by consolidating control over a key AI infrastructure component, potentially biasing the platform toward Nvidia's hardware and software interests. Despite these concerns, Hugging Face's CEO views the deal as an opportunity to expand the user base significantly, while Nvidia's investment promises to support the platform's capital-intensive operations, including storage and bandwidth demands.

item.title: Study finds 35% of new websites by mid-2025 contain AI-generated or AI-assisted text, with increased semantic similarity but no clear drop in factual accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers from Imperial College London, Internet Archive, and Stanford University analyzed a representative sample of websites from 2022 to 2025 to assess the prevalence and impact of AI-generated text on the internet. They found that by mid-2025, about 35% of newly published websites were AI-generated or AI-assisted, a rise from zero before ChatGPT's launch in late 2022. The study observed increased semantic similarity and positive sentiment in AI-generated content but did not find statistically significant evidence of decreased factual accuracy or stylistic diversity. The team used multiple AI detection methods and surveyed US adults about their perceptions of AI's impact, revealing a divergence between public concerns and measured effects. Their findings suggest that while AI-generated text is becoming widespread and influencing online discourse, some feared negative impacts like truth decay are not yet supported by data.

item.title: Bruce Schneier presents 'Hacking AI' at DEF CON 34, addressing AI system vulnerabilities and security challenges [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: At DEF CON 34, security expert Bruce Schneier delivered a presentation titled "Hacking AI," focusing on the vulnerabilities and security challenges inherent in artificial intelligence systems. He explored potential attack vectors on AI technologies and highlighted the need for robust security measures to safeguard AI applications from exploitation.

item.title: Mistral launches Agentic Search to improve AI-driven document navigation and retrieval with higher accuracy and lower latency [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Mistral has introduced Agentic Search, a retrieval layer designed to enhance AI systems' ability to navigate, read, and verify information within complex documents. The technology supports sensitive domain-specific data and integrates with existing search indexes to deliver more accurate results while reducing latency and token usage, as demonstrated by significant improvements on FinanceBench and OfficeQA Pro benchmarks. Agentic Search addresses limitations of traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by enabling multi-step retrieval loops that allow AI models to iteratively search, inspect, and verify information across multiple sources. This approach helps enterprises unlock value from proprietary and confidential data stored behind isolation boundaries, improving AI performance on dense, multi-document queries that require reasoning beyond single-pass retrieval.

item.title: Hacker News discussion questions the value of code reviews for AI-generated code and whether to trust or rewrite AI output [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Hacker News thread debates the necessity and effectiveness of conducting code reviews on code produced by AI tools. Participants express skepticism about reviewing AI-generated code, suggesting either writing code manually or accepting AI output without review. The discussion highlights uncertainty about best practices for handling AI-assisted coding and the role of human oversight.

item.title: Comparison of the 1990s World Wide Web and today's advanced AI technologies highlights evolution in computing capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The 1990s featured the early World Wide Web with simple websites and limited interactivity, while today's technology landscape is dominated by sophisticated artificial intelligence systems capable of natural language processing, image recognition, and autonomous decision-making. This shift reflects decades of progress in computing power, data availability, and algorithmic development.

item.title: Pew Research finds 10% of English-language webpages show AI authorship signs in 2026, rising to over one-third for pages published after ChatGPT's 2022 release [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pew Research analyzed nearly half a million English-language webpages from the past five years using AI detection tools and found that 10% of pages in a July 2026 sample showed significant signs of AI authorship. This share rises to over one-third when considering only pages published after ChatGPT's release in late 2022, reflecting a growing trend in AI-generated or AI-edited online content. The study also found that AI-authored text is unevenly distributed across web domains, with about 10% of .com pages showing AI signs compared to lower rates on .org, .edu, and .gov domains. Linguistic patterns such as frequent use of em dashes, Oxford commas, and certain vocabulary terms were identified as common features of AI-generated writing. These findings highlight the increasing presence of AI in shaping internet content and raise questions about authenticity and trust online.

item.title: Google DeepMind launches WeatherNext 3, an AI weather model using real-time satellite data for hourly, high-resolution global forecasts integrated into Google Search, Maps, and Cloud [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google DeepMind has introduced WeatherNext 3, its most advanced AI weather forecasting model that uses real-time satellite data to deliver hourly, high-resolution predictions globally. The model offers forecasts five times sharper than its predecessor, improving accuracy for temperature, precipitation, and wind patterns. WeatherNext 3 is integrated across Google Search, Maps, Gemini, and Google Cloud, enhancing weather information accessibility for users and developers. Unlike traditional physics-based simulations with data lags, WeatherNext 3 learns directly from live satellite observations, enabling rapid updates and precise local forecasts at resolutions as fine as 5 kilometers. This advancement supports better planning in agriculture, renewable energy, and daily activities by providing timely and detailed weather insights worldwide.

item.title: Pangram emerges as leading AI text detection tool amid debate over its reliability and impact on publishing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pangram, a Brooklyn-based AI startup, has gained prominence as a top tool for detecting AI-generated text, claiming to estimate the percentage of AI involvement in writing. The company has been involved in high-profile cases where its detection influenced publishing decisions, including the cancellation of a novel's release and scrutiny of major publications. Founded in 2023 by former Google and Tesla employees, Pangram uses techniques like synthetic mirroring and hard negative mining to train its models, serving industries such as education and legal sectors. Despite its growing adoption, Pangram faces skepticism from some writers and experts who question the trustworthiness and fairness of AI detection software. The company emphasizes its use of properly licensed datasets and aims to address concerns about AI's impact on creative fields, but debates continue over the accuracy and consequences of labeling content as AI-generated. Pangram's role in the evolving landscape of AI content detection highlights ongoing tensions between technological innovation and creative integrity.

item.title: NVIDIA drives AI boom with key technology contributions fueling sector growth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: NVIDIA is playing a central role in advancing artificial intelligence technologies, significantly contributing to the current expansion and development of the AI industry. Its innovations in hardware and software have become foundational to AI research and commercial applications, supporting a wide range of AI-driven products and services.

item.title: Ask HN: How do developers prevent AI agents from getting stuck in repetitive apology and response loops [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Hacker News discussion explores methods to stop AI agents from repeatedly apologizing and restating the same information. Contributors share various strategies aimed at improving AI conversational flow and reducing redundancy in responses.

item.title: Multiplayer AI Manifesto proposes principles for collaborative AI agents to reduce context loss and improve productivity across enterprise workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The Multiplayer AI Manifesto outlines five principles aimed at enabling AI systems to operate collaboratively across multiple users and tools, addressing the limitations of siloed AI chats. It emphasizes open, shared agent sessions that integrate with existing work platforms to reduce context switching and improve organizational learning and security. The manifesto highlights challenges such as the "context tax" caused by isolated AI interactions and the risks of AI agents acting without enterprise-wide security controls. It cites studies and examples, including a Harvard Business School experiment and Shopify's internal AI system, to demonstrate the productivity gains from multiplayer AI. The manifesto calls for AI agents to continuously improve, share knowledge, and automate routine communication to allow humans to focus on higher-value tasks.

item.title: Epoch.ai launches FrontierMath Erdős benchmark to rigorously evaluate AI on selected unsolved Erdős math problems using formal verification and open-source tools [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Epoch.ai has introduced FrontierMath Erdős, a new benchmark designed to measure AI capabilities in solving selected unsolved math problems posed by Paul Erdős. The benchmark focuses on 68 problems curated for their mathematical significance and difficulty, aiming to provide a more rigorous and transparent evaluation framework for AI math performance. The initiative addresses challenges in curation, verification, and replicability by collaborating with mathematician Thomas Bloom for problem selection, using the Lean proof assistant for formal verification of AI-generated solutions, and open-sourcing the entire benchmark codebase. This approach seeks to improve transparency and reliability in tracking AI progress on complex mathematical problems.

item.title: Nvidia confirms $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face to strengthen AI platform influence, CEO says it won't limit AI chip choices [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia has confirmed its $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, a prominent open-source AI model repository widely used by developers to build and customize AI applications across various chips. Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang stated the company does not plan to restrict developers' choice of AI chips despite the acquisition. Meanwhile, competitor Broadcom forecasts significant growth in AI chip revenue by 2027-2028, highlighting the expanding AI hardware market.

item.title: Nvidia launches Personal AI Router (PAIR) to connect local RTX, DGX, and Mac devices for private AI inference clustering [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia has introduced the Personal AI Router (PAIR), a software solution that connects compatible Windows, macOS, and Linux systems with NVIDIA RTX GPUs and DGX Spark systems into a personal AI cluster. PAIR enables these devices to share local AI inference workloads across the network while keeping data private and on-premises. PAIR supports routing AI tasks across multiple devices without requiring special hardware setups, allowing users to maximize local compute resources for AI applications and agents. It integrates with existing local inference backends like Ollama and LM Studio and operates without sending prompts or files to the cloud, preserving user privacy.

item.title: BotPool Create launches AI-powered chat tool to build and publish websites and apps with human expert support [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: BotPool Create offers a new AI-driven platform that lets users build websites and applications by describing their business and needs through chat. The AI designs, writes, and assembles the site, allowing users to refine it conversationally before publishing on a free subdomain with SSL and SEO features included. The platform integrates a marketplace of over 26,000 human experts who can take over site customization beyond AI capabilities without rebuilding. BotPool Create provides free hosting, version history, spam-protected contact forms, and options to connect custom domains on paid plans, aiming to simplify web development for users without coding or design skills.

item.title: The Economist profiles NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's influential role in advancing AI technologies and shaping the industry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has been recognized for his significant impact on the artificial intelligence industry, drawing comparisons to cultural figures due to his leadership in AI development. The Economist explores how Huang's vision and strategic decisions have positioned NVIDIA at the forefront of AI innovation, influencing both technology and market dynamics. This profile highlights Huang's role in driving AI advancements and shaping the future direction of the field.

item.title: Meta tests and refines its upcoming Hatch AI agent to prevent unsafe behaviors before launch [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Meta Platforms is preparing to launch Hatch, a new personal AI agent designed to assist users with tasks ranging from health to finances. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has emphasized the importance of ensuring the agent's safety and reliability before release. The company has conducted extensive internal testing, known as dogfooding, to identify and fix undesirable behaviors in Hatch. These efforts aim to enable the agent to act effectively on users' behalf while minimizing costly mistakes, with the launch expected in the coming weeks.

item.title: Crew launches iOS apps for its multiplayer AI workspace enabling collaboration between humans and AI agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Crew is a multiplayer AI workspace designed to facilitate collaboration between humans and AI agents on projects. The platform, originally available for MacOS and Windows, has now expanded its accessibility by launching dedicated iOS applications, allowing users to engage with their projects on Apple mobile devices. Crew operates locally without requiring accounts or servers, supporting shared or local workspaces and enabling users to connect multiple AI agents through their own CLI accounts. The platform includes features like multi-agent threads, ticket boards for project planning, token usage tracking, and integrated tools such as file explorers, terminals, and synchronized music playback to enhance collaborative workflows.

item.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Astra model with advanced commercial and cybersecurity capabilities, suggests potential for AGI [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has launched its new GPT-6 Astra model, highlighting significant improvements in commercial applications such as financial modeling and engineering design. The company also noted the model's enhanced cybersecurity features and initially plans limited availability. The release marks a major step in OpenAI's AI development, with the company suggesting that GPT-6 Astra could represent progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). Details on broader deployment and specific use cases remain limited at this stage.

item.title: Snowflake reports 28% growth in CoCo coding assistant users as enterprises seek AI tools beyond Anthropic models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Snowflake's latest quarterly report highlights growing enterprise demand for AI coding tools that integrate multiple models rather than relying solely on Anthropic. The company's CoCo coding assistant, which uses Anthropic and OpenAI models, saw a 28% increase in customer accounts in the July quarter, reaching 9,100 accounts. Snowflake is also expanding CoCo's capabilities by adding open-weight and open-source models like DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3 to offer more cost-effective and flexible AI solutions for corporate CIOs.

item.title: Anthropic prepares IPO prospectus amid investor demand for detailed AI-specific financial metrics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic is set to release its initial public offering prospectus after Labor Day, marking the first time public investors will see a comprehensive financial overview of the AI company behind Claude. While private investors have had access to growth and revenue projections, public investors are seeking more detailed information beyond standard financial statements. Executives at Anthropic have engaged in discussions with potential large investors about providing additional AI-related business metrics, such as AI tokenomics, revenue per gigawatt of compute, and net revenue retention rates. However, it remains uncertain whether the company will disclose these specific performance indicators in its IPO filings.

item.title: Abliteration.ai offers commercial access to open-weight AI models with removed guardrails for offensive cybersecurity and red-teaming tasks [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Abliteration.ai has launched a service providing access to powerful open-weight AI models stripped of safety guardrails, including Z.ai's GLM-5.3, to support offensive cybersecurity, red-teaming, and agent testing. The startup hosts these modified models via web and API, aiming to enable defenders to replicate harmful behaviors for improved security, though the removal of safeguards also facilitates potentially dangerous uses. The company, founded in late 2025 and incorporated in March 2026, operates without venture capital funding but has deals with major cloud providers and offers a moderation layer for customers to add guardrails. Critics warn that abliterated models could be misused for harm, with experts suggesting government intervention through content classifiers and customer identity verification. Abliteration.ai acknowledges the challenge of balancing access and responsibility as it develops further safety measures.

item.title: Meta offers up to 95% discount on Muse Spark AI model usage in exchange for sharing prompts and outputs to improve future models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Meta has introduced a contributor pricing model for its Muse Spark AI model, which is designed for coding and agent operations. Under this model, users who share their prompts and model outputs receive discounts averaging about 95%, significantly lowering the cost of input and output tokens compared to standard pricing. This approach aims to gather valuable user data to enhance future AI models, addressing challenges Meta has faced in obtaining training data. The company's pricing guide suggests the contributor tier is intended to facilitate prototyping and scaling experiments where training on user data is acceptable, potentially encouraging companies to reconsider which data they share with model providers amid growing competition in AI pricing and capabilities.

item.title: OpenAI commits $1 billion to Daybreak initiative providing AI cyber defense tools and training for frontline defenders of essential services [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has launched Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, a $1 billion global initiative to expand subsidized access to advanced AI cyber defense models, training, and technical support for organizations protecting essential services such as water, electricity, local government, and banking. The program prioritizes resource-constrained defenders in the United States and plans to extend support internationally through partnerships and the Daybreak Defense Network. The initiative addresses the growing threat of AI-enabled cyber attacks by equipping defenders with tools to identify vulnerabilities, analyze suspicious activity, and develop fixes before attackers exploit weaknesses. OpenAI's commitment includes a pilot with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center and aims to help defenders manage complex and aging infrastructure systems with limited budgets and expertise.

item.title: OpenAI launches Astra, its most powerful AI model with advanced cybersecurity and coding capabilities, available to Daybreak and paid plan users [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced Astra, its latest AI model, claiming it offers unmatched speed, accuracy, and safety for computer and browser tasks. The model is initially available to Daybreak cybersecurity customers and will roll out to other paid plans and API users over the following week. OpenAI president Greg Brockman described Astra as the company's most intelligent and aligned model, representing a significant advancement in AI delegation and empowerment. Astra features enhanced cybersecurity abilities, including identifying zero-day exploits to aid defenders, and excels in software engineering benchmarks compared to previous models. However, Astra's use of opaque recurrence, which obscures the chain of thought monitoring process, has sparked controversy. OpenAI acknowledges the challenge of monitoring more capable models and frames some opacity as a natural evolution. While Astra's release prompted questions about artificial general intelligence (AGI), OpenAI clarified that AGI is no longer a contractual milestone but a conceptual idea, leaving its classification open to interpretation.

item.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI AI chatbots experience simultaneous outages with unclear causes on September 3 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, and xAI's Grok all faced outages on the morning of September 3, disrupting their AI chatbot services. While xAI attributed its Grok outage to a compute center issue in Memphis, OpenAI cited a routing error, and Anthropic did not disclose specific causes. The outages coincided but were not linked to a shared third-party provider, as major cloud and internet infrastructure companies reported no issues. OpenAI and Anthropic have not confirmed any common source for the disruptions, and xAI apologized to affected compute partners amid its ongoing partnership with Anthropic and SpaceX.

item.title: WIRED reports George Santos banned for life from Kalshi and Google engineer arrested for Polymarket insider trading amid prediction market controversies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: WIRED's Uncanny Valley podcast covers recent high-profile incidents in prediction markets, including former US representative George Santos receiving a lifetime ban and fine from Kalshi for alleged bet manipulation, and a Google engineer facing insider trading accusations at Polymarket. The episode also discusses the reconstruction of Flock's AI-powered police search tool and debates over how to discuss rogue AI agents online. Santos was banned and fined after allegedly manipulating a bet on his attendance at the State of the Union, while the Google engineer claims his actions were mere gambling. Reporters reverse-engineered Flock's surveillance technology, which has faced criticism for misuse by law enforcement. The hosts also explore the online backlash surrounding discussions of AI agents that bypass safeguards and coordinate attacks on other systems.

item.title: Researchers identify interpretable symptom vectors for depression in a large language model, aligning internal activations with clinical assessments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed the internal activations of the Gemma-3-27B-PT large language model to understand how depressive symptoms are represented, finding that symptom groups separate distinctly at a specific model layer. They used mechanistic interpretability techniques and Semantic Projection to map naturalistic text onto symptom vectors derived from validated clinical instruments, preserving clinician-annotated symptom rankings across mood, somatic, and suicidality dimensions. A single depression vector at layer 21 effectively distinguishes depressive from non-depressive text, suggesting potential for interpretable depression-assessment tools based on model activations.

item.title: Researchers introduce Sparse Readout Prism to explain logit-lens scores via sparse readout features independent of corpus fitting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), a method that decomposes the readout matrix of language models into sparse features to explain logit-lens scores without relying on corpus fitting. SRP reveals stable readout features that provide a new unit of analysis beyond token identities and reconstructs more logit differences than existing baselines. This approach addresses corpus conditionality by offering a corpus-independent control for analyzing intermediate hidden states in language models.

item.title: Study finds large language models generate less diverse outputs than their training data across multiple model families and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed large language models including OLMo, Pythia, and GPT-Neo to compare the conditional entropy of their outputs with that of their training data, revealing that model-generated outputs consistently exhibit lower diversity. This conditional diversity gap was also observed in other generative models such as class-conditioned ImageNet generators and text-conditioned models trained on MS-COCO. To address this, the study proposes a post-hoc correction method that generates multiple outputs per input and reweights them using a matrix-entropy projection, increasing output diversity while staying close to the original model distribution. The researchers provide an information-theoretic framework and a scalable algorithm to measure and mitigate this diversity gap in generative models.

item.title: Researchers propose TaRA method to improve Low-Rank Adaptation initialization by aligning low-rank gradients with full-rank model gradients for better fine-tuning performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Training-aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization (TaRA), a method designed to enhance Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by initializing it so that gradients from low-rank factors closely match those of the full-rank weight matrix. This approach addresses sensitivity in LoRA performance caused by initialization and the information bottleneck from low-rank decomposition. TaRA is derived from a mathematical formulation and adds minimal computational overhead. Across various fine-tuning tasks, TaRA consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art initialization methods, offering a simple, robust, and scalable solution for effective LoRA initialization.

item.title: Researchers introduce Declarative Attention protocol enabling language models to control their own attention, reducing token processing by up to 52% with minimal accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Declarative Attention (DA), a new protocol that allows language models to declare which parts of the context to attend to during generation, partitioning attention into global, focus, and local modes. This approach reduces the need to read the entire key-value cache, significantly cutting the number of tokens processed during decoding. Evaluated zero-shot on 15 long-context tasks using off-the-shelf models like Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-27B, DA reduced total attended tokens by 52.0% and 31.1% respectively, with modest accuracy drops that decrease as model size increases. DA introduces a new form of sparse attention with potential for further improvements through training-based methods in future research.

item.title: Researchers analyze how misleading context corrupts medical question answering in large language models, testing fabricated evidence and assertions on 8,627 MedMisBench questions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how misleading context affects large language models' medical question answering by injecting fabricated evidence and bare assertions into 8,627 clinician-reviewed questions from MedMisBench. They tested three reasoning models, finding all were more susceptible to assertions than fabricated evidence, with misleading cues disclosed more often in reasoning traces than in final responses. The study revealed that fabricated evidence corrupts reasoning early and accumulates, while assertions redirect conclusions near the end. An open model's reasoning trace allowed a monitoring system to detect 78% of corrupted decisions at 5% false positives, outperforming detection from responses alone. The findings highlight that the most misleading contexts are disclosed least and are detectable mainly through open reasoning traces, which are often withheld by frontier providers.

item.title: Researchers introduce influence-guided response rewriting to enhance training data attribution effects in large language models, showing stronger behavioral shifts than traditional reweighting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Training data attribution (TDA) seeks to identify which training examples influence model behavior, but its effectiveness depends on both the examples chosen and how they are modified. Researchers found that influence functions (IF), which estimate changes under small reweighting, often yield limited impact when used for reweighting interventions. To address this, they propose influence-guided response rewriting, replacing responses of influential examples with behavior-aligned or opposed supervision while keeping instructions fixed. This method was tested across four open-weight large language models using epistemic abstention as a benchmark, producing stronger, more persistent, and bidirectional behavioral changes compared to reweighting the same examples.

item.title: Researchers introduce HEART framework with Tool Primitives and ToolFace repository to improve LLM tool use, achieving up to 85% API cost reduction and outperforming leading models on benchmarks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Tool Primitives, a design replacing rigid API schemas with natural language interfaces for tool invocation in large language models (LLMs), enabling nested and multi-turn tool calls. They also introduce ToolFace, a centralized repository of over 25,000 functions that LLMs dynamically access to retrieve relevant tools during inference, avoiding the need to list all API schemas. Building on these, the HEART framework combines a Planner, Router, and Verifier to support dynamic tool invocation, multi-step execution, and feedback-driven recovery. Experiments across five benchmarks show HEART outperforms supervised fine-tuned models by 10% on average and surpasses GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro by 6%, while reducing API costs by up to 85%. On 50 real-world tasks, HEART achieves 84% task completion, significantly higher than the 22% average of three leading commercial models.

item.title: Researchers present two techniques to improve realism in AI alignment evaluations by using inference-time compute and deployment-like agent harnesses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers address the challenge of evaluation awareness in AI alignment by introducing two methods that make simulated evaluations more similar to real deployments. The first method, critique refinement, uses additional inference-time compute to generate and refine multiple candidate actions for more realistic simulation. The second method, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target model in an agent harness to better mimic real deployment environments in coding tasks. Testing on multiple models shows that combining both techniques yields greater realism improvements than using either alone. These automated approaches enhance the effectiveness of alignment evaluations by using extra compute more efficiently than simply extending audit duration.

item.title: Researchers propose scalable Kronecker-Fisher approximation for efficient Hessian analysis in billion-parameter language models, revealing key vulnerability patterns and aiding compression strategies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a scalable Kronecker-based approximation method that enables practical Hessian analysis of billion-parameter language models without storing the full Fisher matrix. This approach identifies consistent vulnerability patterns, notably high sensitivity and strong cross-layer correlations in value projection layers across multiple model families, while other components show architecture-specific behaviors. The team conducted extensive experiments involving quantization, sparsification, inter-layer corruption, and fine-tuning after corruption, demonstrating that their approximation correlates strongly with both performance degradation and recovery. This framework offers a theoretically grounded tool for pinpointing fragile components in large models, facilitating guided compression and optimization techniques such as mixed-precision allocation, layer-wise sparsity, and adaptive low-rank decomposition at both layer and weight group levels.

item.title: Loom introduces embedding-space reweighting to aggregate free-text diagnostic hypotheses for root cause analysis, achieving faster inference with competitive accuracy on OpenRCA benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Loom is a generative consensus framework designed to combine noisy and conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable consensus for root cause analysis (RCA) in industrial NLP applications. It projects modular heuristic-generated hypotheses into a continuous embedding space and uses an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm to resolve conflicts, followed by a single lightweight large language model (LLM) synthesis step. Evaluated on the OpenRCA benchmark, Loom matches or closely trails state-of-the-art autonomous agents across multiple datasets while significantly reducing inference latency by approximately 26 to 33 times compared to heavier LLM synthesizers. The framework bridges the gap between traditional weak supervision methods, which are limited to discrete classes, and monolithic LLM agents that face context and latency challenges. Deployment experiences highlight trade-offs between agentic depth and inference speed, challenges in redundancy detection, and the benefits of deterministic consensus in building trust among subject matter experts.

item.title: Researchers find substantial incoherence in language model probabilistic forecasts using Dutch-book analysis on stock return events [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated the coherence of probabilistic forecasts generated by language models using a method based on de Finetti's theorem and Dutch-book analysis, which measures the guaranteed profit an arbitrageur could make betting against the model's probabilities. They applied this method to forecasts on events derived from stock returns data without requiring outcome labels, allowing assessment even when outcomes are unresolved. The study found significant incoherence in language model forecasts, which worsened with more complex logical relationships between events and irrelevant contextual details. The researchers suggest that alternative training strategies may improve the probabilistic coherence of language models.

item.title: Researchers develop Nemotron-3 models that surpass gold-medal thresholds in IOI coding competitions using post-training and feedback-driven refinement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present a specialization pipeline combining problem curation, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and a feedback-driven test-time strategy called GenCorrect to enhance large language models for competitive programming. Using 22,000 curated problems, they trained Nemotron-3-Nano-CC and Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC models, achieving scores exceeding gold-medal thresholds at IOI 2025 and 2026. The Ultra-CC system scored 535.4 out of 600 at IOI 2026 under human-like constraints, surpassing the top human contestant's score of 498.27. This marks the first AI system to outperform the highest-scoring human on an IOI problem set.

item.title: Beyond Transfer Accuracy: Mechanism-Guided Controlled Adaptation for Low-Resource Languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2601.08146v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing circuit discovery methods rely on templated tasks with clean counterfactuals, limiting their use on diverse natural text. We adapt Contextual Decomposition for Transformers (CD-T) for unstructured settings via label-balanced activation means and task-directional relevance scoring, enabling counterfactual-free circuit discovery. We leverage the discovered circuits for Circuit-Targeted Supervised Fine-Tuning (CT-SFT), restricting parameter updates to task-relevant heads and LayerNorm. Experiments on NusaX cross-lingual sentiment transfer show that CT-SFT is highly competitive for low-resource adaptation. While non-circuit sparse updates and full fine-tuning sometimes match target accuracy through capacity recruitment, CT-SFT most consistently avoids catastrophic forgetting, preserving source-language and related-task performance. Extensions to XNLI support the source-retention and intervention findings on a harder task and two model families, showing that circuit-targeted adaptation provides a more controlled, intervention-supported alternative to global fine-tuning.

item.title: ICE: Intervention-Consistent Explanation Evaluation with Statistical Grounding for LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.18579v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating whether explanations faithfully reflect a model's reasoning remains an open problem. Existing benchmarks use single interventions without statistical testing, making it impossible to distinguish genuine faithfulness from chance-level performance. We show that faithfulness is not a fixed property but an operator-dependent quantity that changes with the intervention method used to measure it. We introduce ICE (Intervention-Consistent Explanation), a framework that evaluates explanations against random baselines of equal size under multiple operators. Evaluating 7 LLMs across 4 tasks with deletion and retrieval infill operators, we find that switching operators crosses the positive-evidence threshold in 18% of configurations (5 of 28 attention comparisons), with gaps reaching 44 percentage points. Randomized baselines detect anti-faithfulness (explanations worse than random) in nearly one-third of English deletion configurations, invisible without random comparisons. These patterns persist across 6 non-English languages and 2 attribution methods. The methodology generalizes to step-level chain-of-thought evaluation, where preliminary results on 3 frontier models suggest that high accuracy does not imply faithful reasoning.

item.title: Agentic Scaffolding Amplifies Sycophantic Behavior in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.21377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models, the tendency to prioritize user agreement over truthful responses, has been documented extensively but studied primarily in single-turn settings. This paper investigates a critical question: does subjecting LLMs to greater interaction scaffolding make sycophancy better or worse? Across 4,800 veracity judgments (200 statements $\times$ 6 models $\times$ 4 conditions), we find that the interaction scaffolding characteristic of agentic systems (feedback loops, reconsideration checkpoints, and iterative refinement) systematically amplifies sycophantic behavior. Multi-turn interaction, user pressure, and iterative self-refinement each provide additional opportunities for models to drift toward agreement, and this drift coincides with a mean accuracy drop of $-6.3$ percentage points, establishing the capitulation as harmful rather than corrective. More capable models show larger amplification effects, a troubling inversion of expectations. We introduce the concept of agentic sycophancy amplification (ASA) and two novel metrics: capitulation rate and sycophantic capitulation rate. Our results indicate that as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, sycophancy becomes compounding rather than merely persistent. Systems designed with human oversight loops may inadvertently create the conditions for this drift.

item.title: The Illusion of Replacement: Rethinking Specialized Machine Learning Models in the Foundation Model Era [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.28980v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can the specialized architectures that machine learning has traditionally built for structured data be replaced by language-based models? This question is examined through a review of 159 papers (2016--2026) across nine modalities, with predictive accuracy considered alongside structural representation and computation. A distinction is made between performing a task and preserving and computing the structure that makes the task tractable, and existing approaches are organized into eight representational regimes, ranging from language-only systems to fully specialized architectures. Language-mediated models are found to be highly competitive in specific settings, including extreme few-shot prediction, discretized symbolic tasks, textually annotated knowledge graphs, and large-scale single-modality pretraining. However, whenever structural representation or computation is directly evaluated rather than accuracy alone, no evidence of general architectural replacement is found. Instead, a recurring pattern is observed across independent research communities: when language alone is insufficient, the missing structure is reintroduced through a graph module, structural tokens, specialized attention, or another non-linguistic component. In this sense, specialization more often relocates than disappears. Moreover, although performance of language-based models is improved by scaling, whether the gap to a structure-aware architecture can eventually be eliminated remains untested. The official repository for this work is available at https://github.com/kiyan-rezaee/language-vs-structure.

item.title: Language Diffusion Models are Associative Memories Capable of Retrieving Unseen Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2604.26841v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When do language diffusion models memorize their training data, and how to quantitatively assess their true generative regime? We address these questions by showing that Uniform-based Discrete Diffusion Models (UDDMs) fundamentally behave as Associative Memories (AMs) $\textit{with emergent creative capabilities}$. The core idea of an AM is to reliably recover stored data points as $\textit{memories}$ by establishing distinct basins of attraction around them. Historically, models like Hopfield networks use an explicit energy function to guarantee these stable attractors. We broaden this perspective by leveraging the observation that energy is not strictly necessary, as basins of attraction can also be formed via conditional likelihood maximization. By evaluating token recovery of $\textit{training}$ and $\textit{test}$ examples, we identify in UDDMs a sharp memorization-to-generalization transition governed by the size of the training dataset: as it increases, basins around training examples shrink and basins around unseen test examples expand, until both later converge to the same level. Crucially, we can detect this transition using only the conditional entropy of predicted token sequences: memorization is characterized by vanishing conditional entropy, while in the generalization regime the conditional entropy of most tokens remains finite. Thus, conditional entropy offers a practical probe for the memorization-to-generalization transition in deployed models.

item.title: SABER-Math: Automated Benchmark for Information Retrieval Evaluation in Mathematics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.29894v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As agentic AI systems tackle more complex mathematical tasks, they increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) to search problem databases, theorem libraries, and educational resources. However, choosing the right retriever remains difficult, as it is infeasible to directly isolate its effect on downstream performance. On the other hand, existing retrieval-specific benchmarks often fail to capture fine-grained mathematical relevance, penalizing relevant documents. We address this gap by introducing SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark for evaluating mathematical IR without expert annotation. Starting from 283K high-school-level math problems with solutions, SABER-Math builds challenging reranking tasks in three steps: (i) first, LLMs extract concise solution summaries and mathematical topics for each problem; (ii) then, per-query relevant documents are discovered using ontology topic-based and lexical solutions-summary-based similarities, and (iii) finally, a Swiss-style LLM preference tournament produces fine-grained relevance ratings for the documents. We evaluate lexical retrievers, specialized mathematical retrieval systems, and recent embedding models. We find that while modern embedding models substantially outperform classical and math-specific baselines, even the strongest systems struggle in symbol-heavy domains like Algebra and Calculus. Importantly, we show that general-purpose IR benchmarks such as MTEB do not reliably predict mathematical performance, especially for recent embedding models, highlighting the need for math-specific retrieval benchmarks.

item.title: Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy: Learning Autonomous Policies from Imperfect VLM Teachers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.01567v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide useful priors for interactive decision-making, but using them directly as policies is expensive and brittle: they must be queried at every step, do not improve from environment interaction, and can repeat systematic errors. We study how to learn a cheap autonomous policy from an online, expensive, and imperfect but informative VLM teacher. We propose SAGE (Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy), a framework that queries a VLM only when the learner is uncertain, executes the suggested action during training, and distills guidance into a lightweight Reinforcement Learning (RL) policy. Because VLM advice is not always reliable, SAGE can weight teacher-action distillation using environment-derived advantages rather than treating all suggestions as equally useful. Across sparse-reward visual reasoning and navigation tasks, SAGE learns policies that act without VLM guidance at evaluation time and improves over unguided RL in several environments, including settings where the learned policy exceeds its VLM teacher. The results show that selective guidance is most beneficial when the VLM can help the agent discover high-reward trajectories, and less useful when unguided exploration already succeeds or teacher actions do not lead to informative experience. SAGE also reduces VLM usage by prompting the teacher only on a fraction of training steps and requiring no VLM calls at deployment. Overall, our results suggest that VLMs don't need to be used as fixed policies to be useful; they can instead act as temporary, imperfect sources of guidance whose value is tested and internalized through interaction.

item.title: PRO-Step: Step-level Process Reward Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.01658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation enhances Large Language Models by grounding responses in external knowledge, but multi-hop reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, where early retrieval failures confound subsequent steps. Standard outcome-based optimization only rewards the final answer, leaving intermediate retrieval and reasoning errors undetected. While existing process-based methods introduce step-level signals, they still score each step against the final answer, rewarding spurious successes where flawed retrieval coincidentally produces the correct answer. Step-level supervision in RAG requires evaluating both logical validity and evidential grounding at each step. We introduce PRO-STEP: we train a generative PRM that evaluates both dimensions, employ PRM-guided value tree search to construct preference pairs contrasting valid steps against flawed ones, and optimize the policy via step-level Direct Preference Optimization. Experiments on single and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that PRO-STEP achieves the best average EM and F1 across five benchmarks. Code, models, and training data are publicly available at https://github.com/keemminnke/PRO-Step.

item.title: VakyArth: Evaluating Pragmatic Competence in LLMs across Indic Languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.01788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world communication often requires pragmatic reasoning: interpreting meanings implied through context and cultural convention rather than stated literally. Existing pragmatic evaluation remains largely limited to English and high-resource languages, leaving Indic languages unexplored despite their linguistic and cultural diversity. We introduce VakyArth, the first pragmatic benchmark for Indic languages, designed as a diagnostic evaluation covering Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam. VakyArth evaluates models across five phenomena: deixis, speech acts, implicature, social pragmatics, and coherence; through multiple-choice questions, natural language inference, and translation, with all items authored by native speakers. Across multilingual large language models (LLMs) of varying families and sizes, we find consistent failures on pragmatic meanings rooted in Indic linguistic and cultural conventions. Our analysis shows systematic differences across languages and tasks: MCQ accuracy exceeds NLI accuracy in all model-language combinations, translation performance does not reliably track pragmatic understanding, and Indo-Aryan languages show a translation advantage over Dravidian languages. We further show that automatic translation metrics can miss fluent but pragmatically unfaithful outputs, especially for implicature and deixis.

item.title: Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.01867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A major question in cognitive modeling concerns the behavioral alignment between large language models and humans across linguistic and non-linguistic tasks. Unlike standard LLMs, large reasoning models (LRMs) are optimized with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, encouraging correct solutions to reasoning tasks rather than preference-aligned responses. Recent work (de Varda et al., 2025) investigates the cost of thinking in humans and LRMs by comparing human reaction times with model reasoning traces across a range of reasoning tasks. We isolate this alignment by turning to abductive reasoning: unlike deductive tasks, its difficulty cannot be inferred from formal structure and offers no shortcuts a model could exploit to mimic effort without genuine search, providing firmer ground for empirical claims of shared effort. We find further evidence of alignment between LRM and human reasoning effort, as well as evidence that models and humans tend to make similar errors. Finally, we show that decoding methods that let models explore multiple reasoning paths increase alignment in reasoning cost between humans and LRMs across the three models tested.

item.title: IDEEA: training-free Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steering aligns large language models (LLMs) by injecting a bias into selected activations at inference time, offering a far cheaper alternative to weight-update methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. However, most existing training-free steering methods are input-independent: a single direction is fitted once and shared across all inputs. This is fundamentally limiting as different inputs occupy different regions of the activation space and admit different optimal steering directions toward the same target concept, much as the gradient with respect to a fixed loss varies from input to input. We close this gap with IDEEA (Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching), a training-free framework for input-dependent steering. IDEEA clusters the positive and negative activation supports per attention head, and solves an optimal-matching problem to construct a set of cluster-conditional directions, all about the target concept. At inference time, it picks from this pool of directions and uses the one that best matches the input's own activation for steering. IDEEA aligns the model toward the target concept while preserving the input's original representation, evidence that activations encoding a concept occupy several distinct sub-regions of the representation space rather than a single one. IDEEA improves the truth $\times$ info rate in TruthfulQA by an average of 9.9% (up to 23.5%) over the best input-independent baseline.

item.title: Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to the auto-regressive paradigm. With bidirectional attention and any-order generation, DLMs naturally fit infilling tasks, which require generating a middle span conditioned on both the prefix and the suffix. However, infilling is sensitive to the length of the span, while DLMs require the length to be fixed before generation. Although prior studies extend DLMs to dynamic lengths, they still suffer from two limitations. (i) Sensitivity to initial length. These methods require a preset length to initialize the search and are highly sensitive to this initial length, often yielding suboptimal results. (ii) Inference inefficiency. They either insert length-changing operations during generation or repeatedly search for an appropriate length using multi-step denoising confidence, both of which introduce substantial extra forward passes and computational cost. Therefore, we propose PILL (Probing-based InfiLling with preset-Length-free decoding), an efficient infilling method for DLMs that requires no preset initial length and adds far fewer extra forward passes than baselines, substantially reducing inference time. Experiments show that, across five DLMs spanning different families, architectures, and training recipes on eight infilling benchmarks, PILL improves over the strongest baseline by +4.8 average pass rate on code and +6.0 BLEU-2 on text, while running 1.82x faster than that baseline. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsu1023/PILL.

item.title: text2ql: Multi-Target Natural Language Querying via a Language-Agnostic Intermediate Representation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural language interfaces to databases have traditionally suffered from three structural limitations: exclusive targeting of relational SQL, unconditional dependence on large language model (LLM) inference at query time, and absence of any runtime signal when generated queries are semantically incorrect. This paper presents text2ql, an open-source Python framework that addresses all three limitations through a language-agnostic Intermediate Representation (QueryIR) and a pluggable renderer architecture. A single seven-stage detection pipeline serves both SQL and GraphQL targets; a zero-LLM deterministic mode delivers 100% execution accuracy at a median latency of 3.2 ms with no API cost; and every generated query carries a runtime confidence score in [0.15, 0.97] computed from an additive signal model. Evaluated on 50-query random samples from the Spider and BIRD benchmarks (indicative results; full-set evaluation is planned), the LLM-backed mode achieves 62-70% exact match and 84-91% execution accuracy; the deterministic mode achieves 100% execution accuracy with zero parse errors across all 100 test cases. An ablation study isolates schema-aware prompting as the dominant accuracy lever, contributing +18.4 percentage points of exact-match gain over the schema-free baseline on both benchmarks. text2ql is publicly available at https://pypi.org/project/text2ql/ under the Apache 2.0 license.

item.title: C$^{3}$T: Counterfactual Causal Reasoning for Sentiment Shifts in Social-Media Conversation Trees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sentiment in social-media threads does not only vary across posts; it shifts as users react to claims, corrections, evidence, and hostility within a branching reply tree. We study why sentiment changes in rumor-centric conversation trees by treating discourse moves (e.g., denial/correction, evidence/link, toxicity/attack) as candidate interventions and asking (i) what sentiment a reply expresses, (ii) whether the sentiment shifts relative to its parent, and (iii) which prior message most plausibly drove the reply's sentiment. To support this setting, we introduce CaSiRe, a causal sentiment reasoning layer over public rumor conversation datasets that adds post-level sentiment labels, induced parent-child shift labels, calibrated multi-label intervention tags, and explicitly annotated causal-source labels. We then propose C$^{3}$T (Counterfactual Causal Conversation Transformer), a thread-structured temporal model that jointly predicts node sentiment and shifts, learns sparse ancestor attribution, and supports counterfactual queries by forcing conversational intervention embeddings on or off to estimate potential outcomes. Under an event-level split, C$^{3}$T improves out-of-event robustness and attribution over text-only, graph-based, and temporal baselines, and yields interpretable model-based effects: denials/corrections and evidence reduce downstream negativity, while toxicity increases it. We also benchmark open-weight LLM prompting baselines and find that added conversational context helps, but attribution remains less reliable, motivating structure-aware counterfactual modeling for social-media analysis.

item.title: OBJECTION! Lawyer Agents Mitigate Guilty Bias in Legal Judgment Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) models are typically trained on documents that describe facts from a prosecutorial perspective. Existing datasets further exhibit severe label imbalance toward guilty outcomes. Consequently, these models suffer from "Guilty Bias", blindly accepting the prosecution's narrative as objective truth. Previous studies employing three-step reasoning structures or training on synthetically generated innocence data improve overall accuracy, but they still fail to mitigate bias at inference time. In this paper, we introduce OBJECTION, an inference-time pipeline that integrates an Adversarial Lawyer Agent into each 3-step reasoning of offense, unlawfulness, and culpability. Unlike generic critics, our agent actively challenges the model's presumptions of guilt by injecting legal defense arguments at each reasoning stage. To thoroughly evaluate this, we present a new "Natural Innocent" dataset including 3.4k real-world cases, overcoming the limitations of synthetic innocence benchmarks. Test results show that OBJECTION drastically reduces the False Guilty Rate (FGR) from 82.93% (SOTA baseline) to 16.69%, proving its capability to perform substantive legal reasoning. This work denotes a key progress toward aligning Legal AI with the presumption of innocence.

item.title: Breadth Beats Depth: Improving GCG-Based Jailbreak Optimization with Breadth-Oriented Suffix Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimization-based jailbreak attacks such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) achieve strong effectiveness and transferability by optimizing adversarial suffixes on white-box source models. However, existing GCG-based methods rely on averaged adversarial loss and deep greedy search, which can over-emphasize easy-to-jailbreak behaviors and overlook promising regions of the suffix space. We propose BOSS, a plug-and-play framework that improves GCG-based jailbreak optimization through breadth-oriented suffix search. BOSS uses Tail-Focused Adversarial Loss (TFAL), standard source loss, and behavior coverage to select terminal suffixes, then explores multiple short trajectories and selectively continues promising suffixes. Experiments on public benchmarks show that BOSS improves attack success rates across multiple GCG-based methods while reducing optimization time.

item.title: PaperCompiler: Faithful Paper-to-Code Generation via Repository-Level Specification Compilation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Faithfully translating research papers into repository-level implementations remains challenging because papers often describe methods at a high level, leave implementation assumptions implicit, and require generated repositories to preserve method logic, evaluation protocols, and cross-file consistency. Despite recent advances in paper-to-code agents, their intermediate outputs are often presented as free-form plans or summaries that downstream coding agents may ignore, reinterpret, or compress, leading to algorithmic simplification and inconsistent repository structure. To address these challenges, we introduce PaperCompiler, a paper-to-code generation framework that compiles paper-grounded evidence into explicit repository-level implementation specifications. PaperCompiler grounds implementation-relevant evidence while preserving source provenance and distinguishing paper-supported, inferred, externally delegated, and unresolved information. The resulting specifications encode non-degradation requirements, ownership assignments, cross-file dependencies, and file-level constraints. Repository generation proceeds under these compiled specifications while retaining flexibility over local engineering choices not fixed by the paper. PaperCompiler outperforms strong baselines on Paper2CodeBench, achieving a 13.8% relative improvement in reference-based fidelity (from 3.64 to 4.15) and reducing high-severity evaluator critiques (from 13.2% to 6.1%).

item.title: DiffIE: Diffusion-based Open Information Extraction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A single sentence often expresses multiple valid relational triplets, which makes Open Information Extraction (OpenIE) fundamentally a multi-output task. Existing neural systems handle this by autoregressive generation, which is flexible but slow and prone to redundancy, or by fixed-slot prediction, which is efficient but couples the extraction budget to training. We introduce DIFFIE which instead treats the stochasticity of conditional discrete diffusion as the extraction mechanism itself: independent reverse-diffusion trajectories over per-token role tags produce a pool of candidate triplets, which are clustered under lenient matching and ranked to form the output. Both the pool size and the number of returned extractions are inference-time choices, decoupling the extraction budget from training and exposing test-time compute as a tunable axis. DIFFIE achieves the new state of the art in CaRB (1-1) both F1 and AUC, and outperforms the strongest rule-based system (ClausIE) in BenchIE; it also remains competitive in standard CaRB and WiRe57 evaluations, giving the best average score among systems that report all four benchmarks. Ablations show that uniform discrete diffusion outperforms absorbing state diffusion in our setting, and that a matched non-diffusion stochastic tagger does not reproduce its gains. Our results indicate that diffusion stochasticity is an effective mechanism for structured prediction tasks with multiple valid outputs.

item.title: NE-R1: Enhancing Named Entity Recognition Model via Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) has achieved substantial progress since the advent of large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, the recognition of long-tail and domain-specific entities remains challenging due to the deficiency in parametric knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offers a promising remedy by injecting external knowledge, but it also introduces noise and unnecessary cost when dealing with familiar cases. In this paper, we propose NE-R1, a novel framework for adaptive retrieval-augmented NER. We design a "retrieval-on-demand" mechanism for NER. Then we integrate it into models by a two-stage training method: (1) multi-task instruction tuning initialization; (2) end-to-end RL optimization with CoT. To achieve reasonable selection between parameterized and external knowledge, we design a multi-dimensional reward considering both accuracy and retrieval benefit. NE-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, with an average F1 score gain of 2.52% in in-domain evaluation and 1.18% in zero-shot cross-domain evaluation.

item.title: MultiGhostBench: A Multilingual Benchmark for Long-Form LLM-Generated Text Attribution under Distribution Shifts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While existing work on LLM authorship attribution (AA) has made progress, available benchmarks remain limited, often focusing on English, controlled settings, or relatively outdated models, with the few multilingual studies considering only relatively short texts. We introduce MultiGhostBench, a multilingual benchmark comprising 928 books generated by five recent LLMs across six languages and three scripts, with an average length of approximately 59K words per book. The benchmark supports evaluation under domain, author, and language shifts. Evaluation of representative AA methods shows that no single method consistently performs best across settings, and performance generally degrades under distribution shifts. Transformer-based detectors can retain generator-related information across languages, although transfer effectiveness varies by language pair, whereas statistical and fingerprint-based detectors are more language-dependent. We envision MultiGhostBench as a valuable resource for the development and evaluation of robust AA methods. The dataset and code can be found at https://github.com/GrecoMT/MultiGhostBench.

item.title: PolERo: Studying Political Evasion in Romanian [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Political evasion refers to responses that engage with a question while withholding the requested information. Recent NLP work frames political evasion as a classification task using a two-level taxonomy of response clarity and fine-grained evasion strategies. Existing work on response clarity and evasion classification is limited to English, leaving open whether the taxonomy and model behavior transfer across languages and political contexts. We introduce PolERo, a dataset of 3,574 human-annotated question-answer pairs extracted from official transcripts of five Romanian presidents. We evaluate multiple classification approaches on both datasets under matched conditions, including TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned encoder models, a proposed sliding-window encoder, and zero/few-shot LLM prompting. We study cross-lingual transfer through joint bilingual training and machine-translation-based data augmentation. Our results indicate that fine-tuned encoders are competitive, cross-lingual transfer is asymmetric, and ambivalent evasion categories involving pragmatic cues remain the main challenge across all model families.

item.title: Before the Script, Set the Stage: How Worldview Simulation Amplifies Psychologically Grounded Persuasion in Multi-Turn Jailbreaking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks demonstrate that harmful intent can be distributed across dialogue, yet existing methods obscure what conversational mechanisms drive vulnerability. We introduce BLUEPRINT, a safety-evaluation framework separating a factorized social-influence strategy space from WORLDVIEWSIM, a cross-turn situational context module. Monte Carlo Tree Search optimizes turn-level combinations of 18 theory-grounded influence factors across a four-turn trajectory. Across six frontier models, BLUEPRINT achieves near-ceiling ASR on major open-weight and proprietary models, while requiring the fewest average queries (2.46). The resulting trajectories further reveal model-specific vulnerability among resistant targets: each responds to distinct influence factors and strategy transitions, yet all share a common recovery pathway-shifting toward concrete, executable task framing consistently escapes hard-refusal states. Ablations confirm operational cues matter most: making requests actionable has the largest impact, gain framing is unusually potent, and some legitimacy appeals can backfire. These findings suggest robust multi-turn safety requires monitoring not only harmful content, but also how dialogue state makes unsafe requests appear concrete and locally executable.

item.title: When Decodability Is Not Enough: Logical Validity Representations, Behavioral Dissociation, and Causal Tests in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can look capable of logical reasoning, but correct or incorrect answers alone tell us little about what the model represents internally. We study logical verification in five open-weight transformer models using matched valid--invalid premise--claim pairs that vary across inference families, semantic domains, templates, and difficulty levels. Despite near-chance behavioral performance, logical validity is often almost perfectly decodable from hidden states and remains strongly decodable under held-out templates, domains, and inference families. Validity also remains highly decodable on behaviorally incorrect examples in the conditions where correctness-conditioned evaluation is well defined.
